issues.subcategory: inconsistent scale anchors for frequency measure
issues.description: The text describes the modified frequency scale inconsistently across sections. The substance use section states the scale runs 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day), while the pornography section states 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day), and the gambling section also says 1 (never) to 6. The supplemental materials code frequency as 0-5 (Never=0 to More than Once Per Day=5). This discrepancy matters because centering, interaction terms, and the interpretation of coefficients depend on the actual coding, and replicators cannot know which scale was used.
issues.quote: participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)

issues.subcategory: inconsistent count of moderation analyses and outcomes
issues.description: The manuscript variously refers to 'eight proposed outcomes,' '8 target behaviors/variables,' and '10 moderation analyses,' but the enumeration is inconsistent. There are 7 behaviors/substances (pornography, gambling, alcohol, tobacco/nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, illicit drugs), with pornography and gambling each having two outcome measures, yielding 9 outcome-measures, not 8 or 10. The internal arithmetic does not reconcile, creating ambiguity about the confirmatory analysis set.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling repeated for both the NIDA-ASSIST measure and the validate measures of problematic use

issues.subcategory: inconsistent SESOI/Cohen's d values
issues.description: The smallest effect from Grubbs, Lee et al. is reported with conflicting d values: 'Cohen's d = .22' in one sentence and 'Cohen's d = .25' for what is described as the same effect (β=.11, ΔR2=.012, f2=.016). These cannot both be correct for the same effect, and since the SESOI is anchored on this value, the inconsistency undermines the justification of the equivalence region.
issues.quote: to small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen’s d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen’s d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)

issues.subcategory: conflation of standardized beta with Cohen's d as equivalence bound
issues.description: The SESOI/equivalence region is set at δ=|.11|, which is described as 'the observed standardized estimate (β value).' However, equivalence tests for regression coefficients (Anderson-Hauck / reg.equiv.fd) operate on a standardized regression coefficient metric, and the authors elsewhere treat this same .11 value as if interchangeable with Cohen's d. Standardized regression coefficients and Cohen's d are not the same metric, and conflating them when defining the equivalence bound can misspecify the equivalence interval and bias the equivalence conclusions.
issues.quote: we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen’s d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)

issues.subcategory: non-equivalent operationalization of the moderator across the key comparison
issues.description: The SESOI is anchored on an effect for the interaction of RELIGIOUSNESS (not moral disapproval) with frequency, yet the confirmatory hypotheses concern the interaction of MORAL DISAPPROVAL with frequency. The authors acknowledge religiousness and moral disapproval are different constructs, but still use the religiousness-based effect to define the equivalence bound for moral-disapproval interactions. Because the central claim is the uniqueness of moral incongruence (disapproval×frequency), benchmarking against a religiousness×frequency effect introduces a construct mismatch into the inferential anchor.
issues.quote: Notably, this effect was observed for an interaction between religiousness (as opposed to moral disapproval directly) and pornography viewing frequency in predicting self-reported addiction.

issues.subcategory: outcome measure does not match the 'addiction/dysregulation' construct for substances
issues.description: For substances, the 'problematic use' outcome is the average of NIDA-ASSIST items that themselves include socially/morally loaded content (e.g., a friend or relative expressing concern, failure to control, legal/financial problems). Several of these items are confounded with social disapproval and moral framing, so an association between moral disapproval and this outcome could be partly tautological rather than reflecting true dysregulation. This threatens the construct validity of the central contrast between sexual and non-sexual addictions.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be standardized, and an average will be taken for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.subcategory: non-comparable outcome scales undermine cross-domain comparison
issues.description: The core inferential goal is to compare the magnitude of the moral incongruence interaction across pornography vs. gambling vs. substances. However, the outcomes differ substantially: BPS (summed, 6-month window), PGSI (averaged, 12-month window), and NIDA-ASSIST averages (3-month windows, mixed response scales). Differing reference periods, scoring (sum vs. average), and item content make standardized coefficients non-comparable across domains, directly threatening the validity of the uniqueness claim that depends on cross-domain magnitude comparison.
issues.quote: These will be included to allow fully parallel analysis across behaviors and substances (i.e., everything will be on the exact same scale using the exact same measurements).

issues.subcategory: confirmatory hypothesis effectively requires accepting the null
issues.description: Hypotheses 2b and 3b predict that the interaction will fall within the equivalence region (i.e., be practically null) for gambling and substances. The validity of this confirmatory inference depends entirely on adequate power for equivalence at the very small SESOI (f2=.015). By the authors' own Table 2, prescription drug misuse (n≈140) and illicit substances (n≈240-480) are underpowered (achieved power .301 and .472-.764) to support equivalence at the SESOI, meaning the predicted 'practically zero' conclusion cannot be validly supported for these subgroups.
issues.quote: However, we do not expect to find that the interactions of self-reported substance use frequency with moral disapproval of those substances will contribute uniquely to predicting self-reported problems with or addiction to those substances.

issues.subcategory: contingent redefinition of equivalence region introduces researcher degrees of freedom
issues.description: The authors pre-specify that if effects exceed the equivalence region or if power is insufficient, they will redefine the equivalence region using the lower bound of the 95% CI of the pornography effect (variously β=.23 or based on a different study). Switching the equivalence bound after seeing results, and choosing among multiple candidate anchors (.11, .145, .23, .27), constitutes substantial analytic flexibility that can manufacture support for the uniqueness claim regardless of outcome.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: vague, post-hoc decision rule for assumption violations and model choice
issues.description: The plan to switch from OLS to DWLS latent variable models is gated on whether assumptions are 'substantially' violated, with no pre-specified quantitative threshold for 'substantial.' This leaves a researcher degree of freedom in which analytic pipeline is reported as primary, especially relevant because sign/significance of the interaction drives the central conclusions.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate

issues.subcategory: multiple comparisons not addressed for confirmatory interaction tests
issues.description: The study conducts approximately 9-10 confirmatory moderation/equivalence tests plus numerous covariate effects, yet no correction for multiple comparisons is specified for the focal interaction tests (Holm adjustment is mentioned only for bivariate correlations). Without controlling family-wise error or false discovery across the focal tests, the probability of at least one spurious significant or spurious-equivalent result is inflated, which is especially consequential given the directional uniqueness claim.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

issues.subcategory: single-item moral disapproval measures lack reliability assessment
issues.description: Moral disapproval for every behavior is measured with a single item, and frequency is also single-item per behavior. The reliability of these key predictors cannot be estimated, and measurement error in the components attenuates and biases the interaction term (which is central to the equivalence tests). The manuscript discusses computing alpha/omega only for multi-item scales, leaving the focal predictors' measurement properties unassessed.
issues.quote: we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement “I believe that using ________ is morally wrong” on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: inconsistent moral disapproval scale anchors
issues.description: The substance moral disapproval item is described in the main text as a 7-point agreement scale, but the response anchors used elsewhere (1 strongly disagree to 7 strongly agree) and the equivalence between substance and pornography items must be verified; the main text says items 'match previous measures' but prior work sometimes used different scaling. Additionally, the manuscript does not report how the moderator is scaled relative to the original validated pornography moral disapproval items, which is needed to interpret comparability of standardized estimates.
issues.quote: we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography. For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement

issues.subcategory: unsupported assumption of no missing data
issues.description: The authors assert they anticipate no unplanned missingness and will not need to remove any responses based on YouGov's proprietary standards. This is implausible for self-report survey data on sensitive behaviors and provides no missing-data handling plan (e.g., for skipped items, refusals, or panel attrition). If missingness occurs, there is no pre-specified approach (e.g., FIML, multiple imputation), threatening the integrity of the confirmatory analyses.
issues.quote: Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: no attention/validity checks despite reliance on third-party guarantees
issues.description: By disclaiming any data screening for careless or inattentive responding and relying entirely on the vendor's unspecified 'proprietary' standards, the study forgoes independent quality control. Without described attention checks or screening criteria, undetected low-quality responses could bias both the interaction effects and equivalence conclusions, and the procedure cannot be evaluated or replicated.
issues.quote: certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards

issues.subcategory: PGSI response options omit the value 1 / mislabel scale
issues.description: The PGSI is described as a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always) in the main text, but the supplemental response coding is Never (0), Sometimes (2), Most of the time (4), Almost Always (5). These codings are mutually inconsistent (0-3 vs. 0/2/4/5) and the supplemental coding is non-standard for the PGSI (which is typically 0-3), affecting scale scoring and comparability with published norms.
issues.quote: on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: BPS response scale inconsistent between main text and supplement
issues.description: The main text describes the Brief Pornography Screen as a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often), but the supplemental materials code responses as Never (0), Occasionally (2), Very Often (4). The 0/2/4 coding contradicts the 0-2 description and would change the summed score range and the validated cutoffs, undermining replicability and comparison to the validated measure.
issues.quote: on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: NIDA-ASSIST two-item scoring labels inconsistent
issues.description: The two yes/no-style ASSIST items are described in the main text with anchors '0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months,' which is a 3-category scale mislabeled as a '3 point scale' with values 0/3/6. Mixing these 0/3/6-coded items with 0-5 frequency items and then standardizing/averaging across heterogeneous response metrics is not justified and the inconsistent labeling impairs replication.
issues.quote: for each substance on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months)

issues.subcategory: alcohol binge item mislabeled in supplement
issues.description: The supplemental binge-drinking items are gender-branched (4 drinks for women, 5 for men) but both tables label the single response row 'More than four drinks (1)' even under the 'IF GENDER = MAN / more than 5 drinks' header. This labeling error creates ambiguity about what was actually administered and scored.
issues.quote: In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion?

issues.subcategory: sports-betting oversample biases gambling prevalence and effects
issues.description: 1,500 of ~4,000 participants are recruited specifically for past-year sports wagering, and Table 2 lists gambling 'Effective N' of 3,325 combining a 73% national rate with a 100% sports-betting oversample. This oversampling makes the gambling subsample non-representative and inflates gambling engagement, which can distort the gambling moderation/equivalence estimates and compromise the cross-domain comparison and any population-level generalization for gambling.
issues.quote: Gambling | 73%  (national sample) 100%  (sports-betting oversample) | 3,325

issues.subcategory: confirmation-oriented framing of confirmatory hypotheses
issues.description: The introduction and present-study sections repeatedly state the explicit goal of 'demonstrating' that moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior, rather than testing it neutrally. Framing a confirmatory registered report around demonstrating a desired conclusion (and labeling a disconfirming outcome 'especially unlikely') signals confirmation bias that can influence analytic choices, particularly the contingent redefinition of the equivalence region.
issues.quote: with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors

issues.subcategory: diagnostic/clinical implications drawn from cross-sectional population data
issues.description: The discussion proposes that confirming hypotheses would support the ICD-11 clinical caveat for CSBD and the diagnostic uniqueness of moral distress. However, the data are cross-sectional, non-clinical, and based on self-reported feelings of addiction rather than diagnosed disorders. Extending population-level correlational interaction findings to validate a clinical diagnostic criterion overstates what the design can support, even though the authors note treatment-seeking populations are where the effect matters most.
issues.quote: should hypotheses be confirmed, there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD

issues.subcategory: frequency restriction (users only) changes the interaction interpretation
issues.description: Problematic-use and moral-disapproval items are administered only to past-year users of each behavior, so the moderation models are estimated within users only, with variable and behavior-specific subsamples. Conditioning on use changes the meaning of the frequency×disapproval interaction and induces non-comparable selection across domains (e.g., 3.5% prescription misusers vs. 70% drinkers), complicating the cross-domain uniqueness comparison that is the study's core aim.
issues.quote: key measures will be restricted to those who have engaged in the behavior within the past year. That is, we will only administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to participants who report engaging in those behaviors.

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency scoring/aggregation underspecified
issues.description: The main text states gambling frequency will be formed as 'an average across gambling behaviors,' implying multiple gambling-activity items, but the supplemental instrument contains only a single gambling-frequency item ('Gambled or placed bets at all'). It is therefore unclear what is being averaged, which affects both the predictor's construction and replicability.
issues.quote: To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: standardized estimate comparability across logistic/skewed outcomes not addressed
issues.description: Many outcomes (e.g., prescription/illicit drug problems among small user subsamples, PGSI) will be highly skewed/zero-inflated. The plan compares standardized β interaction estimates across these outcomes, but standardized coefficients are sensitive to outcome variance and distribution. Without addressing distributional non-comparability, the cross-domain magnitude comparison and the equivalence tests (which assume a meaningful common standardized metric) may be biased.
issues.quote: Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction for moral disapproval of a behavior and frequency of that behavior fall fully within our equivalence region, we may reasonably conclude that the true effect is so low as to be null or practically null

issues.subcategory: gender operationalized as binary contradicts panel measurement
issues.description: Analyses code gender as binary (1=male, 0=not-male), but the supplemental gender branching uses 'WOMAN'/'MAN' categories and the panel provides a 'Gender' variable of unspecified categories. The collapsing rule (non-male grouping) and treatment of non-binary or missing gender responses are not fully specified, affecting covariate adjustment and replicability.
issues.quote: Interactions will be tested using this program with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: covariate set may be insufficient to isolate moral incongruence
issues.description: The models adjust only for age, gender, and religiousness. Yet self-reported problems and moral disapproval may be jointly influenced by other confounds (e.g., general distress/negative affect, impulsivity, socioeconomic status, social desirability). Omitting such confounds threatens the interpretation of any interaction as reflecting 'moral incongruence' specifically, particularly given the ASSIST outcome items' social-disapproval content.
issues.quote: we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates, as prior work has demonstrated clear links between such variables and self-reported problematic pornography use

issues.subcategory: abstinence/never-user exclusion limits population-level claims
issues.description: Because moral disapproval and problem items are only collected from users, individuals who morally disapprove strongly enough to abstain are excluded from each behavior's analysis. This selection removes the part of the moral-incongruence spectrum most relevant to the theory (high disapproval) and may bias the interaction toward null for substances with low prevalence, undermining the population-level generalization the authors claim.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

issues.subcategory: Table 2 illicit substance figures internally inconsistent
issues.description: Table 2 lists illicit substances at 6%-12% prevalence with Effective N 240-480 and smallest detectable f2 of .032-.016, but the text elsewhere states illicit drug prevalence as '6%-12%' while the power narrative sometimes treats illicit and prescription thresholds interchangeably. The range-based entries with single power figures (.472-.764) are ambiguous about which assumption is used for the confirmatory decision, leaving the powered/underpowered determination unclear.

issues.subcategory: missing pre-specified threshold for declaring 'robust' across methods
issues.description: The decision to present OLS as primary depends on results 'remain[ing] robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques).' What happens if sign/significance diverge between OLS and DWLS is not specified, leaving the reporting pathway and primary inference undefined in a non-trivial contingency.
issues.quote: Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results and corresponding graphs in text
